content: CAMEROON ASSOCIATION FOR BIBLE TRANSLATION AND LITERACY (CABTAL)
Language: Kenyang, spoken in the Manyu and Meme Divisions, South West Province.
Society for Kenyang Literature (SKL) P.O.B 108 Mamfe Manyu Division South West Province CAMEROON ASSOCIATION FOR BIBLE TRANSLATION AND LITERACY (CABTAL) B.P. 1299, Yaoundé

The Kenyang lexicon has been compiled primarily for speakers of the the Kenyang language in order to stimulate interest in the use of the written language, to help new readers and writers and to help standardise spelling. It may also be of interest to non-speakers who wish to learn or study the language. The Kenyang language is spoken in both Manyu and Meme Divisions in the South West Province. The proposed alphabet conforms to the General Alphabet of Cameroon Languages, adopted by the national commitee for the unification and harmonisation of the alphabets of Cameroon languages. The lexicon contains more than 2,500 entries, all of which come from Lower Kenyang which is the reference dialect. Each entry consists of the following: the citation form of the Kenyang word, the plural form where appropriate, the part of speech, and a translation of the meaning. Verbs are glossed using the infinitive in English, but in Kenyang they use the imperative as the citation form. A set of appendices is also found including a summary of an overview of the grammar. Work on a lexicon is never finished, and so much co-operation is needed from other native speakers to expand and improve on this lexicon. This lexicon was compiled through the assistance of Mr. Emmanuel M. Nkongho-Etaka, Mr. Andrew Ashu-Eneke and many other villagers. I am very grateful for their assistance.
Special thanks goes to Dr Robert Hedinger, SIL consultant, who read this paper and made a lot corrections. Without him, this lexicon would not have been completed.

The focus of the present work is the lexicon of Kenyang. However, it is impossible to discuss the lexicon without looking at some of the morphosyntactic structures.
Kenyang is a noun class language with a subject, verb and object (SVO) word order. Simple sentence structures are shown below:

The noun phrase may consist of a noun as head, followed by modifiers such as adjectives and/or determiners. Adjectives in Kenyang are relatively few in number; most are realised in Kenyang with a separate stative clause (e.g. Üthe stone is hardÜ or Üthe stone which is hardÜ, as opposed to the hard stoneÜ). Nevertheless, there are true adjectives for the semantic fields of numbers and colours (see 5.5). Noun phrases may also consist of NP-NP constructions in which the first NP ÜpossessesÜ the second NP. In Kenyang just as in many Niger-Congo languages, this construction is marked by an associative marker (often only tonal) between the possessor and the possesed. The tone may be H or L. Typical noun phrases are as follows:
N + adj N + N bɛtɔk bɛ́pay ɛte ńnok villages two pot soup 'two villages' 'a pot of soup'

Nouns can be divided into several groups or ÜclassesÜ which are distinguished by their prefixes. These classes are numbered according to the system used in all studies of Bantu languages. The class of each Kenyang noun with its corresponding plural is shown in the lexicon, for example `ŋv` 'b`s' belongs to class 3 and its plural form a`ŋv` belongs to class 6. This is indicated by (n 3/6) after the noun. Some nouns belong to the plural class only. In the lexicon, a noun will be found in the lexicon under its singular 5 form with its appropriate prefix [e.g. the word for chief is listed under leɔ and not under eɔ (the noun root) and not under a`eɔ (plural form)].
Here is a list of noun classes with their prefixes and examples:

class 3 a- class 6 ba- aŋwa 'cat' baŋwa 'cats' atá 'cheek' batá 'cheeks'
class 7 ɛ- class 8 bɛ- ɛtɔk 'village' bɛtɔk 'villages' ɛswɔ 'ant' bɛswɔ 'ants'

There is a morphophonemic alternation between the stop /b/ and the nasal /m/. When prefixes having the form /ba-/ or /bá-/ precede a morpheme that begins with a nasal consonant, the prefixes become nasalised. Here are a few examples below:

The merger between formerly distinct mV- and bV- prefixes by a general phonological rule makes it difficult to know the original shape of the nominal prefix of class 6. Vowel-initial stems show, however, irregularities which strongly suggest a nasal noun prefix in class 6:

Derivational processes are limited in Kenyang. The formation of a gerund-type verbal noun are from the verb and the formation of an agent are also from the verb. The gerund is formed by adjoining to almost any verb stem - transitive or intransitive - the noun class class prefix ná-. Thus, we derive forms such as the following:

Kenyang has two types of pronouns which are worthy of note: independent and possessive pronouns. Independent pronouns are those which may stand alone (e.g. in answer to a question such as what? or who?). Possessive pronouns are those which make reference to nouns that ÜpossessÜ other (following) nouns. The following chart sets out these pronouns:
1st person mmɛ ɛya bɛsɛ́ ɛyɛsɛ́ 2nd person wɔ ɛyɛ bɛka ɛyɛka 3rd person yí ɛyi bɔ́ ɛyap

Almost all adjectives in Kenyang are derived forms. Most of them are derived from verbs. Adjectives are marked by a prefix which is governed by the noun class of the noun it qualifies. Adjectives are very few in Kenyang. In the lexicon they are represented with the prefix á-
Numerals are used as adjectives. The prefix of the numeral agrees with the noun it follows. This is illustrated below:

kɛnɔŋ kɛ́pay 'two irons' atú ápay 'two ears' bɛkɛt bɛ́pay 'two houses' -bɛ́ tjodf In the lexicon, the numerals take the prefix aɛ́, they do not follow any noun.. This is shown below under the numeral system.

Kenyang distinguishes four tenses and four aspect markers. Under tenses we can distinguish them by their different auxiliaries as will be seen below, while under aspect we can distinguish them by the change from the citation form of the verb that has a high tone. In Kenyang, the most free form of the verb is the imperative. The imperative is thus taken as the citation form of the verb in this study.
The verb twó come is used to illustrate the tense system. The various tenses are used for illustration as seen below:
Near past atwɔ mbʉ́ 'He came (before two days ago.) Far past atwɔ nyáká 'He came (a long time ago.) Future (certainty) a¿chɔŋ twɔ́ 'He will come ' Future (uncertainty) amay twɔ́ 'He may come. Aspect
There follows a list of aspects with the present tense of the verb twó come which are demonstrated below:
Present perfective: atwɔ 'He has come ' Present imperfective: a¿twɔ∆ 'He is coming ' Present habitual: a¿twɔ nɔkɔ 'He usually comes' Present continuous: a¿twɔ∆ 'He is coming'
